name: Cycloastragenol

lead: Cycloastragenol is the sugar-free form of astragaloside IV, a compound from astragalus root. People take it as an anti-ageing supplement, hoping slower cellular ageing shows up as younger-looking skin and more vitality.

The idea is that it activates telomerase, the enzyme that extends the protective ends of chromosomes, which in turn slows cellular ageing. Cell studies report a moderate rise in telomerase activity and animal models show reduced inflammation. A small human study exists on a related telomerase-activator product, and no trial has measured skin or appearance.

paras: It is taken as a daily oral supplement, usually sold as capsules, often as part of a longevity stack alongside other ageing-focused compounds. Users generally describe it as a long-term routine, with any change expected to build gradually over months.

Human safety data are limited and toxicity data are sparse. Telomerase is active in most cancers, so a theoretical concern exists about activating it. The FTC issued a consent order over ageing-reversal advertising for the branded product TA-65. It is sold as a supplement, not an approved drug.

angle.text: Cycloastragenol is marketed as a telomerase activator: the idea is slower cellular ageing, which users hope shows up as a younger look and more vitality. Support so far comes from cell and animal work.

lead: Cycloastragenol is a tetracyclic triterpenoid obtained from the roots of Astragalus species, notably Astragalus membranaceus. It is the aglycone (sugar-free form) of astragaloside IV, a major saponin of the herb used in traditional Chinese medicine.[1][2][3] It is marketed as a supplement ingredient on the claim that it activates telomerase, the enzyme that extends the protective ends of chromosomes.[1]

Wikipedia describes the telomerase-activation claim as not well established: a preliminary study on human T cells reported a moderate increase in telomerase activity, and the clinical significance is uncertain.[1] Most research on the compound is preclinical, covering inflammation, neuroprotection, cardiovascular and cancer models in cells and rodents.[4][5][6][7]
No study found in these sources tests cycloastragenol for facial appearance, skin or hair outcomes in people.
infobox: Astragalus roots; hydrolysis product of astragaloside IV[1][2]

paras: Cycloastragenol has a 9,19-cyclolanostane skeleton with hydroxyl groups at several positions and an epoxy-bridged side chain; it is the aglycone formed when sugars are removed from astragaloside IV.[2] It is poorly soluble in water.[2] It occurs in the roots of Astragalus membranaceus and A. mongholicus, with content varying by origin and growing conditions.[2] Astragaloside IV, the parent glycoside, is converted to cycloastragenol in part by gut-microbial and hepatic metabolism, according to a network-pharmacology study.[3]

According to Wikipedia, Geron patented cycloastragenol, and Telomerase Activation Sciences acquired the rights in early 2013 to develop the TA-65 supplement.[1] The US Federal Trade Commission issued a consent order against Telomerase Activation Sciences over advertising that implied TA-65 could reverse ageing and repair DNA damage.[1] Wikipedia also notes that much supporting material comes from manufacturers and that few high-impact peer-reviewed publications exist.[1]

Proponents and review articles describe telomerase activation, through signalling such as MAPK/ERK, as the main anti-ageing mechanism.[2][8] Preclinical studies also report effects on SIRT1 expression in a brain-ischaemia model,[4] suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in endothelium, cardiac tissue and a psoriasis-like skin model in mice,[5][7][9] and enhanced anti-tumour T-cell immunity in a cancer model.[6] A Maria Blasco study in mice, cited by Wikipedia, found no lifespan extension, some physiological anti-ageing effects and no increase in cancer incidence.[1]

Human data are minimal. One registered trial, completed in 2016 with 48 participants, examined a telomerase activator in relation to retinal amyloid in Alzheimer disease.[10] The sources consulted report no controlled trial of cycloastragenol for appearance or skin ageing. A preliminary in vitro study on human T cells and a 2013 sponsor-funded study of T cells from six participants reported telomerase activation with TA-65; Wikipedia says the clinical significance is uncertain.[1]

Wikipedia states that toxicity testing is limited and human safety has not been adequately demonstrated.[1] Because abnormal telomerase activity features in most cancers, it raises a theoretical but unproven concern about cancer promotion.[1] Cycloastragenol has also been studied for anti-cancer effects in cell models.[6]
